taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native from Oklahoma through Texas into northeastern and central Mexico.
look_here_first: Find a fine, tight small bunch with threadlike sometimes involute blades. A true wild photographed OPEN branched panicle with tiny separate spikelets is now illustrated in three new source-licensed local images. Lindheimer has a larger fountain and a much more contracted densely packed head. Confirm by measuring a mature attached membranous ligule and spikelet; color alone and intermediate hybrid form are not proof.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve documents M. reverchonii in the natural flora. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed field treatment. Travis — USDA ARS herbarium specimen NA0074024 was collected along upper Bull Creek, about 7 mi NW of Austin.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Use exact specimen/local-flora evidence; do not infer counties solely from Edwards Plateau or Blackland Prairie ecoregion presence.

best_field_traits: densely tufted perennial bunchgrass with shallow condensed rhizome
very fine filiform/involute blades about 1–2 mm wide
membranous inner ligule; published lengths vary by treatment (local <1–1.5 mm vs broader 2–4+ mm)
panicle often develops reddish to pinkish-purple cast at bloom
spikelets larger/coarser than Lindheimer muhly, with lemmas roughly 3.5–5 mm
awn usually present and can extend several millimeters
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Muhlenbergia lindheimeri: Lindheimer muhly is much taller and coarser, with much longer ligules and a much larger feathery panicle. Muhlenbergia capillaris: Pink muhly can look similar at a glance but is not a project-native Central Texas taxon; use provenance plus blade/ligule/spikelet details rather than plume color. Muhlenbergia schreberi: Nimblewill has decumbent branching stems that root at lower nodes and forms low mats/patches rather than a compact basal tuft.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole flowering clump with panicle unobscured and ruler for height.
Close collar and true membranous ligule with mm ruler.
Fresh very narrow blade edge / involute cross-section.
Branching panicle and one awned one-flowered spikelet in macro.
Same-season same-scale compare with M. lindheimeri.
morphology_keys.crew_recognition_note: Start with an erect COMPACT basal tuft of extremely thin, often inward-rolled blades, generally smaller than Lindheimer muhly. At bloom, confirm the delicate OPEN branching panicle, often reddish, with one-flowered awned spikelets. Inspect the membranous ligule and the small leaf width on a fresh blade under magnification; color alone is not diagnostic.
morphology_keys.precision_caution: GrassBase and the local Williamson County description disagree on seep muhly's ligule measurements and margin; do not teach a fixed length threshold without measuring a fresh same-specimen opened sheath. Three LOCAL archived wild flowering photographs DO show real open panicles and attached whole spikelets, but no local photo proves a measured inner ligule, excavated shallow rhizome or dissected glume/lemma veins.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Seep muhly tends to be a finer, smaller densely tufted perennial, with very thin often inward-rolled blades and a much more open wispy panicle than Lindheimer's stout large clump and contracted panicle. Its membranous ligule is generally shorter (GrassBase often 2–4[–9] mm versus Lindheimer often 8–15 mm); published local measurements differ, so use measured attached leaf parts plus one-flowered spikelets, never a hard ligule cutoff. Planted M. capillaris and its cultivars can show showier pink plumes but are not evidence of a local wild seep specimen. Parent-hybrid M. ×involuta requires actual hybrid-specific evidence.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Muhly field check — reverchonii
steps: Gallery panels 1–3: true source-determined seep fine leafy tufts; roots and a clean basal crown are HIDDEN. External Bob Harms natural clump (panel 5) and cultivated CC0 garden habit (panel 12) are context, not exposed-root photographs. New panel 4 shows dried OUTER sheath material, NOT opened true ligule.

Gallery panel 6: Bob Harms MURE2-L is the actual blade–sheath/ligule educational reference with a scale, visibly CREDITED but copyright retained and REMOTE; it is not an archived or independently measured local ligule. Do not overlay anatomy arrows on this restricted original.

Gallery panels 7–9: three real locally archived wild seep-muhly flowering views, with OPEN branched panicles and actual attached spikelets. The single-spikelet closeup is NOT a glume/lemma dissection or a measured one-floret unit.

Gallery panels 10–11: Lindheimer muhly, a DIFFERENT species. Panel 10 compares its denser mature inflorescence; panel 11 compares its coarse bunch, not root anatomy. Preserve the different-species labels.

Same-plant field photography: photograph the ENTIRE Hays/target-region wild flowering clump, clear leaf bases by gently moving litter, then expose one SHORT condensed horizontal rhizome and attached fibrous roots with centimeter/mm ruler. Photograph it before and after clearing soil.

On the SAME plant open a mature blade–sheath joint and photograph its actual inner membranous ligule FRONT and SIDE next to a 1-mm ruler. Do not confuse pale older sheath fragments with a ligule; the locally described <1–1.5 mm and GrassBase 2–4+ mm treatments disagree.

Only when open-panicle habit, true leaf ligule and rooted crown fail to separate look-alikes, dissect and photograph a mature spikelet with scale and distinctly resolved two glumes, lemma/awn. When uncertain, use Muhlenbergia sp.; never force M. ×involuta hybrid ID.

Retain Matt's individual CC BY-NC flowering photo for the genuinely noncommercial credited website, subject to exact photo-license compliance. Bob Harms Selected Monocots images are separate educational-use external references, NOT CC licensed or locally mirrored.

seep_condensed_rhizome_photo_plan_202610.regional_morphology: Williamson County botanical treatment describes seep muhly as a densely cespitose bunchgrass but also inconspicuously shallow-rhizomatous: ca. 2 mm horizontal, condensed, repeatedly branched rhizome with adventitious roots at shoots. A tufted appearance does NOT rule out rhizome structures.
seep_condensed_rhizome_photo_plan_202610.photo_priority: ONE same-plant wild Hays/Edwards Plateau clump loosened from limestone soil: shoot bases together with intact shallow condensed horizontal rhizome, adventitious roots from the branch points, and still-attached flowering culm. Millimeter scale beside actual rhizome.
seep_condensed_rhizome_photo_plan_202610.true_ligule_priority: Fresh inner sheath peeled open to reveal membrane and blade base together with an actual millimeter scale; do not reuse unmeasured external Harms photo as new measured locally archived proof.
seep_condensed_rhizome_photo_plan_202610.contrast: Do not label this species a stoloniferous spreading mat merely because there is a short rhizome. The dense cluster of very short branching axes creates a compact bunchgrass. Contrast this morphology with rooting aboveground runners of M. schreberi.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FINE TUFT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Small tight perennial bunch with very fine often rolled blades
field_id_short_tiles.details: Williamson County treatment: a many-stemmed fibrous-rooted bunchgrass with a shallow condensed branched rhizome; blades about 0.6–<2 mm in locally examined plants. Inspect PHOTO 1 for naturally growing fine blades and low clump; PHOTO 2 shows tangled dry and living leaves. The Bob Harms image (gallery panel 5) is a separate credited educational EXTERNAL habitat reference, not an excavated crown. The final CC0 garden photo documents cultivated habit only. None photographs a connected, exposed root/rhizome. New gallery panel 3 shows fresh blades and dead basal sheaths among moss and limestone; roots remain hidden.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LIVE TUFT/HABIT PHOTOS; CONNECTED ROOTS/RHIZOME STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · EXPOSE THE REAL LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Short membranous inner collar, often split; published lengths conflict
field_id_short_tiles.details: The Bob Harms Selected Central Texas Monocots MURE2-L photo (gallery panel 6) is a separate credited EXTERNAL educational reference that actually shows a sheath/blade junction with scale. It is not an archived CC-licensed image or an independently measured specimen; we have deliberately added no over-image arrow. Inspect a fresh same-plant sheath opened on its inner side with a 1-mm ruler. Published ligule reports conflict: local Williamson County <1–1.5 mm, minutely ciliate/splitting; wider GrassBase 2–4 mm or longer. Record which plant/shoot was measured. New gallery panel 4 shows ribbed outer tissue and dry sheath, NOT the free inner ligule.
field_id_short_tiles.status: EXTERNAL COPYRIGHT-RETAINED LIGULE REFERENCE; SAME-PLANT LOCAL MACRO MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · FOLLOW THE OPEN PANICLE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Delicate widely branching head, not a dense Lindheimer plume
field_id_short_tiles.details: Three locally archived exact-source wild flowering panels (Matt #58493566, Sam #4920088, Sam #5077102) show open fine branches, individual spikelet-bearing tips and hand context. These are ACTUAL seep flowering photos; don't confuse the immediately preceding MURE2-L photo with a panicle. Broad panicle color and one seedhead alone do not prove the ID.
field_id_short_tiles.status: OPEN PANICLE PHOTO SUPPORTED; SCALE MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE THE TWO GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Single-flowered spikelet ~2.5–3.5 mm; two shorter one-veined glumes
field_id_short_tiles.details: The Sam Kieschnick wild photo #5077102 (gallery panel 9) displays complete narrow spikelets, but not a disentangled pair of two glumes. Williamson County published specimen describes ~2.5–3.5 mm spikelet body excluding awn, two subequal one-veined glumes ~1.3–2.1 mm. These are published measurements NOT measured on the photograph; save microscopic dissection until a real local look-alike cannot be separated by habit, collar and full head.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · FIND THE LEMMA AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: One three-veined fertile lemma, slender terminal awn usually short
field_id_short_tiles.details: Local treatment: the single fertile lemma is about the length of the ~2.5–3.5-mm spikelet, with three veins and inward-rolled margins over the palea. Its fine terminal awn is described as <2–4 mm in local material; broader treatments may give different ranges. Two short palea tips must NOT be mistaken for separate long lemma awns. A whole spikelet photograph cannot prove lemma venation or the exact awn insertion.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lindheimer = coarser denser plume; nimblewill creeps; hybrid stays held
field_id_short_tiles.details: Gallery panels 7–8 show genuine source-identified wild seep OPEN panicles; panel 10 is the clearly labeled DIFFERENT-SPECIES Lindheimer dense flowering head; panel 11 shows a second DIFFERENT-SPECIES coarse Lindheimer bunch. Panel 9 provides true seep solitary-spikelet context. Use whole-plant texture and branching head before dissections. Nimblewill's low rooting nodes and potential hybrid M. ×involuta remain separately provisional; avoid floral-color/cultivar guesses.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON; MATCHED DIAGNOSTIC PHOTO GAP

grass_species_finalization_20261025.look_here_first: Small tight perennial fine-leaved bunch with an open repeatedly forked wispy panicle and solitary awned spikelets; confirm actual short membranous ligule, measured two-glume spikelet and fertile lemma before deciding against Lindheimer muhly or hybrid.

measured_reproductive_key.growth: Williamson County: inconspicuously rhizomatous, fibrous-rooted small bunchgrass, shoots up to ~40 cm in examined local material; broader treatments report taller.
measured_reproductive_key.leaf: Very narrow blades ~0.6–<2 mm in local treatment, often inward-rolled.
measured_reproductive_key.ligule: Local <1–1.5 mm, minutely ciliate membranous and often splitting; broader GrassBase commonly ~2–4 mm, sometimes longer. Retain discrepancy.
measured_reproductive_key.panicle: Local ~10–17+ cm, 12+ main branches, pedicels ~4–15 mm, one spikelet per tip.
measured_reproductive_key.spikelet: ~2.5–3.5 mm excluding awn, one bisexual fertile floret.
measured_reproductive_key.glumes: Two shorter membranous one-veined glumes ~1.3–2.1 mm; lower generally shorter; floret separates above glumes.
measured_reproductive_key.lemma_and_awn: Fertile lemma about spikelet length, three-veined, inward-rolled over palea; slender terminal awn <2–4 mm in local description; palea faintly two-veined with short tips.
measured_reproductive_key.measurement_note: Published A.C. Gibson Williamson County measurements; not measured from existing photos.
